title: Diagnostic Imaging and Radiology
answer: Detection and triage, synthetic imaging, 3D anatomical models, ultrasound enhancement and radiomics.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Pathology Detection and Scan Triage
children.blurb: Pathology detection and scan triage systems examine medical images such as X-rays, CT scans, MRIs, and pathology slides to flag suspicious findings and order cases by urgency.

children.name: Synthetic Imaging from Existing Scans
children.blurb: Synthetic imaging from existing scans refers to AI systems that create new medical images derived from one or more prior scans, such as generating a contrast-enhanced CT from a non-contrast study, synthesizing an MRI sequence from another sequence, or producing a pseudo-CT from MRI for radiotherapy planning.

children.name: Anatomical Models and 3D Printing
children.blurb: Anatomical models and 3D printing in radiology turn CT and MRI scans into physical, patient-specific replicas of organs, bones, and vascular structures.

children.name: Point of Care Ultrasound Enhancement
children.blurb: Point of care ultrasound enhancement covers AI software that helps a clinician acquire, interpret, and act on ultrasound images at the bedside.

children.name: Radiomics
children.blurb: Radiomics is the high-throughput extraction of quantitative features from standard medical images such as CT, MRI, and PET scans.

sections.body: Diagnostic imaging AI now includes software that flags possible fractures, bleeds, and lung nodules on CT and X-ray scans, and sorts worklists by urgency. Synthetic imaging generates new MRI or CT contrasts from existing scans, reducing repeat acquisitions. 3D anatomical models are built from scans for surgical planning and printed. Point of care ultrasound enhancement uses AI to guide probe placement and improve image quality on handheld devices. Radiomics extracts hundreds of quantitative texture and shape features from images to look for patterns linked to outcomes.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some narrow detection tasks, like finding a lung nodule or intracranial hemorrhage on a noncontrast CT, are mature enough for regulatory clearance and routine use, but they still miss subtle findings and can overcall artifacts. Synthetic imaging is promising but can hallucinate or smooth away small lesions, so it is not a replacement for acquired sequences. 3D printing from AI segmentations works well for bones and large vessels but struggles with small, low-contrast structures. Ultrasound enhancement helps novices but depends on operator and body habitus. Radiomics remains largely research because features are sensitive to scanner, protocol, and reconstruction, and many published models do not replicate. The honest limit is that these tools assist a radiologist; they do not replace reading the actual scan.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader wanting to understand how AI flags disease and prioritizes cases should start with Pathology Detection and Scan Triage, which covers the most clinically deployed tools. Synthetic Imaging from Existing Scans explains how new image contrasts are generated and where they fail. Anatomical Models and 3D Printing moves from pixels to physical objects used before surgery. Point of Care Ultrasound Enhancement addresses a different modality where AI guides non-specialists. Radiomics is the most experimental page, showing how quantitative features are mined for research rather than bedside use. Together they move from detection to generation to physical modeling to handheld imaging to feature extraction.
